PROJECT 01 / MECHATRONICS

Prosthetic Hand (Servo-Actuated)

Built & Tested

As part of the Phoenix Hand open-source prosthetic initiative, I designed and built a tendon-driven prosthetic hand using a single high-torque servo (MG946R) to actuate all five fingers through a shared tendon-routing system, with Force-Sensitive Resistors (FSRs) providing haptic feedback for grip control. I designed a custom hand guard and motor casing in SolidWorks to protect the internal servo components while preserving full finger range of motion.

Design Objectives

  • Protect the high-torque servo motor from mechanical stress and impact
  • Maintain full finger flexion range of motion without restricting tendon paths
  • Achieve a compact, wearable form factor suitable for daily use
  • Design for 3D printability using standard FDM processes

Tools & Techniques

  • SolidWorks: part modeling, assembly constraints, dimensional verification
  • FDM 3D printing for prototype fabrication
  • Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) applied to mechanical stress points, improving grip reliability by 33%
  • Closed-loop Arduino Nano control architecture using FSR feedback for non-destructive object manipulation

Demo

The fabricated assembly successfully housed all motor components within the hand profile, enabling autonomous object manipulation via FSR-triggered haptic feedback.

Next-generation concept — not built. I've researched a more advanced control scheme as a future direction: independent per-finger actuation (five micro-servos) driven by surface EMG (sEMG) signals and a machine-learning classifier, so the hand could respond to actual muscle-activation patterns rather than a simple pressure threshold. This would involve bandpass/notch filtering of the raw EMG signal and feature extraction (Mean Absolute Value, Waveform Length) feeding a classifier trained to distinguish grips like pinch, point, and full fist. To be direct about where this stands: it's a researched theoretical direction only — the built and tested prototype remains the single-motor, FSR-based hand shown above.
PROJECT 02 / SENSOR FUSION

Knee Kinematics & Rehabilitation Tracker

Built & Tested

Co-developed with Erik Kunkel, this device was designed to assist patients recovering from knee injuries — with a primary focus on ACL tears — by monitoring rehabilitation progress in real time. It tracks knee flexion angle and applied leg pressure, alerting the patient when they exceed clinically prescribed safety thresholds. I contributed across both the electronics/sensor-calibration side and the mechanical case design, working jointly with Erik on the enclosure iterations shown below.

System Components

  • 2 accelerometers (thigh and calf segments)
  • 2 FSR pressure sensors (forefoot and heel)
  • Arduino Uno microcontroller

Kinematic Tracking

The accelerometers calculate knee angle by measuring deviation from a 180° baseline established with the patient standing at full extension. During calibration, a 10-unit differential between the thigh and calf readings corresponded to a 90° change in angle — roughly a 9°-per-unit conversion factor. The system continuously classifies flexion into three zones: safe (160°–180°), caution (120°–160°), and danger (below 120°).

Pressure & Load Monitoring

The forefoot and heel FSRs (sharing a 5V rail) distinguish walking, standing, and weight-bearing states. On the injured leg, heel readings above 980 units and forefoot readings above 480 units flag dangerous loading of a bent ACL-injured knee — the most clinically critical condition the device detects, since loading a flexed, injured knee risks re-injury.

Results & Validation

The integrated system correctly classified walking (with toe-off/heel-strike detection), normal standing with even weight distribution, uneven standing with lateral lean, overloading of the injured leg, and seated posture with dangerous knee flexion below 90°. A planned multicolored LED indicator was ultimately removed after it introduced processing overhead that disrupted real-time sensor readings on the Arduino — a tradeoff documented for future iterations using a lower-overhead display or a more capable microcontroller.

PROJECT 03 / RESEARCH — ONGOING

3D Hybrid Bioprinter for Disease Modeling & Cancer Research

In Progress

This ongoing research project, conducted in my role as an undergraduate research assistant, addresses a core limitation in cancer and disease research: 2D petri-dish cultures don't replicate how human cells behave in three dimensions, and animal models often fail to translate to human biology. This system bioprints 3D in vitro tissue constructs that let researchers observe human cells grow and respond to treatment in a realistic 3D environment on the lab bench. The architecture separates macro-scale structural scaffolding from micro-scale living-cell placement, pairing a mechanical extrusion toolhead with a pneumatic Drop-on-Demand (DoD) microvalve.

Demo

Hardware & Firmware Architecture

  • Dual-toolhead Cartesian gantry driven by a BigTreeTech Octopus V1.1 board running custom-configured Marlin firmware
  • Left channel — droplet toolhead: a syringe-fed pneumatic system depositing low-viscosity, cell-laden bioink (green, pictured) through a Lee solenoid microvalve, actuated via a Spike & Hold driver (24V spike / 3.2V hold) to prevent coil burnout
  • Right channel — scaffold toolhead: a mechanical syringe pump extruding the structural hydrogel scaffold
  • Validated an in situ crosslinking assay — depositing dyed CaCl2 micro-droplets into an uncrosslinked alginate scaffold to trigger and visually track ionic gelation

Custom Control Software

I developed a Python "Studio" application for full system control, communicating over serial USB, supporting freeform scaffold/droplet design (beyond fixed grid layouts), a custom G-code compiler with per-layer flow/prime/retract settings, live pneumatic vs. plunger dispensing control, dual-device serial connections for the motor controller and valve driver, and a full manual jog/homing/diagnostics suite. The current build can slice an imported STL directly into a scaffold + droplet toolpath, shown below tracing a test "UTD" pattern with separate stroke paths, drop points, and dead-zone margins mapped out before print.

Materials & Bioink Selection — Primary Research Focus

Material selection is the current center of gravity for this project: the scaffold has to hold its shape and print cleanly, while the droplet phase has to keep cells alive and able to attach and grow. Those two requirements pull in different directions, which is why the system is built around testing multiple material families rather than committing to one bioink early. I built the chart below to map out the materials under consideration by mechanical stiffness against cell viability — the two properties that matter most for choosing a scaffold vs. droplet material.

  • Alginate-based hydrogels (with gelatin/agarose blending) — the primary scaffold candidate, for structure and rapid ionic crosslinking
  • GelMA — a tunable, UV-crosslinked option; stiffness scales with polymer concentration and cure time, giving a wide printable range
  • Pluronic F-127 — a thermo-reversible sacrificial material for vascular channels, not intended to support long-term cell growth
  • Decellularized ECM (dECM) — the most biomimetic option, retaining native protein cues, but needs reinforcement to print reliably on its own
  • Collagen I and Matrigel — under evaluation for droplet-phase cell encapsulation, where biological signaling matters more than structural strength

To go beyond my own plotted data, I compiled reported stiffness and viability ranges for these material families (plus PEG-DA and PCL, two options I'm evaluating for stiffer, more structural applications) from published bioprinting literature. The ranges are wide — these properties depend heavily on concentration and crosslinking method — which is itself the practical takeaway: material choice here is a tuning problem, not a fixed lookup.

The pattern that stands out: natural hydrogels (alginate, GelMA, collagen, dECM) cluster at low stiffness with high viability — good for the droplet/cell phase — while stiffer synthetic or structural materials (PEG-DA, PCL) trade viability for mechanical strength, better suited to scaffold reinforcement than direct cell encapsulation. That's consistent with why this system pairs a soft, cell-friendly droplet material with a stiffer, structurally independent scaffold material rather than trying to find one material that does both.

Current Status

This project is actively in progress. Having validated the core multi-modal printing concept, the current phase is focused on refining gantry/toolhead mechanical movement for higher print precision, finalizing scaffold material selection for reliable, repeatable prints, and preparing to run the first full disease-model print as a proof of concept.

PROJECT 04 / WEARABLE DEVICE

Maternal Vital Monitor

Built & Functional

Developed with a four-person team (Anuj Parikh, Erik Kunkel, Daniel Trujillo, and myself) for a biotech design challenge, the Maternal Vital Monitor (MVM) is a wearable obstetric device that monitors a pregnant woman's heart rate and applied pressure in real time, giving the wearer direct feedback on her health status — aimed at catching early indicators of common maternal health complications such as edema, which can progress to preeclampsia if unaddressed. My role on the team was designing the circuit schematic, wiring the full sensor/display/microcontroller system together, and calibrating the sensor data against reference BPM ranges. The CAD design and finished device shown below reflect a fully working, functional prototype — not a concept-only build.

System Components

  • Arduino microcontroller
  • Heart rate sensor module
  • Force-Sensitive Resistor (FSR)
  • Accelerometer (motion/activity context)
  • Micro OLED display and buzzer for real-time alerts
  • Real-time clock (RTC) module
